subject: Using a Bayesian Bootstrap to Estimate the SE of WAIC/LOO

messages.author: 5ac683287691482a
messages.subject: Using a Bayesian Bootstrap to Estimate the SE of WAIC/LOO
parts:
Dear All,

I came across the following passage in one of Aki’s papers:

The standard error and the corresponding formula for se (elpd waic) have two difficulties when sample size is low … For small n, one could instead compute nonparametric error estimates using a Bayesian bootstrap on the computed log-likelihood values corresponding to the n data points (Vehtari and Lampinen, 2002).

Does anyone have code demonstrating how to apply such a procedure to estimate the standard error of the difference in WAIC/LOO between two models fit using Stan? I understand how to calculate a bootstrap, but found the description in Vehtari and Lampinen (2002) difficult to follow.

Cheers!
Jon

Dear All,

I came across the following passage in one of Aki’s papers:

The standard error and the corresponding formula for se (elpd waic) have two difficulties when sample size is low … For small n, one could instead compute nonparametric error estimates using a Bayesian bootstrap on the computed log-likelihood values corresponding to the n data points (Vehtari and Lampinen, 2002).

Yes there is code available. 
For Matlab you can use bbmean function in GPstuff <http://research.cs.aalto.fi/pml/software/gpstuff/>
For R look Rasmus Bååth's Bayesian bootstrap code and nice examples here <http://www.sumsar.net/blog/2015/07/easy-bayesian-bootstrap-in-r/> and here <https://github.com/rasmusab/bayesboot>. 
For Python see here <https://github.com/ilanfri/StatsML/blob/master/Bayesian_bootstrap.ipynb>
You can probably find something with Google for other languages, too.
Bayesian bootstrap is really simple as it's enough that you are able to sample from Dirichlet distribution, which you can do by sampling from Gamma distribution which you can do if you can sample from uniform distribution.
We probably add Bayesian bootstrap (and demo) to R loo package later.

Aki

 

Cheers!
Jon

messages.author: 5ac683287691482a
messages.subject: Re: Using a Bayesian Bootstrap to Estimate the SE of WAIC/LOO
parts:
Thanks, Aki!
I should have clarified that I had found some resources on the topic prior to posting, but was confused by the implementation. My understanding (based upon the code from loo) is that for WAIC we would be trying to bootstrap the SE of a sum. However, the steps laid out in some of the online tutorials (e.g., http://www.sumsar.net/blog/2015/07/easy-bayesian-bootstrap-in-r/) include warnings that the recommended approach does not work for statistics that change with the sample size (as would a sum). Following the procedure described in those tutorials produces outlandish results if sum() is used. For example, in R:

library(bayesboot)
dat_to_sum = 1:20
sum(dat_to_sum) # 210
bbsum1 = bayesboot(dat_to_sum, sum)
summary(bbsum1) # mean = 41849.69, sd = 4934.334

My understanding is that the issue derives from what this particular tutorial/package refers to as R2 – which is the number of draws from the data for any given iteration. The tutorial recommends including far more than are actually in the data set. Changing this value to equal the number of values in the data set fixes the problem:

bbsum2 = bayesboot(dat_to_sum, sum, R2=length(dat_to_sum))
summary(bbsum2) # mean = 209.568, sd = 35.14253

However, this seems to go against the general advice to use a high R2 value. It is also slower than it might be because it has to do everything via resampling rather than using weights. I struggled with this but believe I have sorted it out. My solution was to define a weighted sum based upon the weighted mean:

weighted.sum = function(x,w){length(x)*weighted.mean(x,w)}
bbsum3 = bayesboot(dat_to_sum, weighted.sum, use.weights = TRUE)
summary(bbsum3) # mean = 210.3058, sd = 25.44693

This approach is faster and produces a tighter HDI. I also realized after the fact that the results appear equivalent to taking the bbsum1 results, dividing by R2 then multiplying by the length of dat_to_sum. In any event, could you confirm that this is an appropriate way to bootstrap the SE of WAIC?

messages.subject: Re: Using a Bayesian Bootstrap to Estimate the SE of WAIC/LOO
parts:
Yes, I also use the weighted mean approach (and then multiply by n). Weights are just samples from the Dirichlet distribution.

I don't know what bayesboot function does, but it seems that it's not as logical as it could be...

BB is not the best way to compute SE of anything. Why not just compute SE=std(x)*sqrt(length(x))? I use BB when I assume that SE is not good description of the uncertainty ie. uncertainty is not well approximated by Gaussian.

And I recommend using LOO instead of WAIC.

Aki
